title: Corrosion: the battery you did not want

concepts.label: corrosion
concepts.definition: A metal being oxidised by its surroundings (metal atoms become ions or oxide), spontaneous whenever an available electron taker sits below the metal on the potential ladder.

concepts.label: oxygen reduction (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻)
concepts.definition: The usual cathodic half-reaction of corrosion in neutral water, E° = +0.40 V: dissolved O₂ takes four electrons and becomes hydroxide; with iron (−0.44 V) it gives E°cell = 0.84 V.

concepts.label: anodic / cathodic site
concepts.definition: Spots on a single piece of metal where oxidation (metal dissolves, anodic site) and reduction (oxygen takes electrons, cathodic site) happen, set apart by small differences such as oxygen supply, scratches or impurities.

concepts.label: corrosion cell
concepts.definition: A short-circuited galvanic cell on one piece of metal: anodic site, cathodic site, the metal itself as the electron path and the water film as the ion path; its energy is lost as heat.

concepts.label: rust chemistry (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O)
concepts.definition: Fe → Fe²⁺ + 2e⁻ at the anodic site, Fe²⁺ + 2OH⁻ → Fe(OH)₂ where the ions meet, then oxygen oxidises iron to +3 giving hydrated iron(III) oxide, a porous flaking crust; overall 4Fe + 3O₂ + 2xH₂O → 2Fe₂O₃·xH₂O.

concepts.label: rusting needs water + oxygen
concepts.definition: A corrosion cell runs only with metal, an electron taker (oxygen) and an electrolyte (water) together; salt adds no reaction but makes the water a better ion path and so speeds rusting.

concepts.label: barrier coating (paint)
concepts.definition: A layer such as paint, grease or enamel that keeps water and oxygen off the metal so that no corrosion cell can form; it protects only while it has no hole.

concepts.label: galvanic corrosion
concepts.definition: When two different metals touch in an electrolyte, the one with the more negative E° becomes the anode and corrodes faster than alone, while the other becomes the cathode and is protected.

concepts.label: small anode, large cathode
concepts.definition: The cathode's whole surface collects oxygen and all those electrons come from the anode, so a small anode joined to a large cathode is attacked intensely and a large anode with a small cathode hardly at all.

concepts.label: sacrificial anode
concepts.definition: A piece of metal above iron on the potential ladder (zinc, magnesium) connected to steel on purpose so that it supplies the electrons and dissolves in the steel's place.

concepts.label: galvanising
concepts.definition: Coating steel with zinc (usually by dipping in molten zinc): a barrier that also acts as a sacrificial anode, so the steel stays protected even where the coat is scratched, unlike tin plate or paint.

concepts.label: cathodic protection
concepts.definition: Preventing corrosion by feeding a metal structure electrons from elsewhere so that its whole surface is a cathode; needs an electrolyte (soil, water) connecting structure and anode.

concepts.label: impressed current
concepts.definition: Cathodic protection driven by an external DC source: negative terminal to the steel, positive terminal to an inert anode; too little leaves the iron corroding, too much makes hydrogen at the steel (2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻).

concepts.label: passivation (oxide film)
concepts.definition: Self-protection of a reactive metal (Al, Cr, Ti) by a dense, adherent, self-healing oxide film a few nanometres thick (Al₂O₃, Cr₂O₃, TiO₂) that seals the surface, in contrast to porous rust; chloride can break the film locally (pitting).

concepts.label: stainless steel
concepts.definition: Iron alloyed with at least about 10.5% chromium, enough for a continuous passive Cr₂O₃ film over the whole surface.

concepts.label: corrosion as a battery
concepts.definition: A metal-anode cell (lemon battery, seawater-activated magnesium cell) uses the same half-reactions as corrosion, with the anodic and cathodic sites separated so that the electrons must pass through an external wire.

electrolysis (driving a reaction with an outside source; pointer only)
Pilling–Bedworth ratio (used as 'oxide takes 2.14 times the volume', not named in the prose)
seawater-activated magnesium batteries with a metal-salt cathode

summary: Running example: a 5.58 g (0.100 mol) iron nail in a glass of water. The potential ladder shows that dissolved O₂ (+0.40 V) is the electron taker for iron (−0.44 V), E°cell = 0.84 V; a water drop on iron then shows rusting as a short-circuited galvanic cell with anodic and cathodic sites, followed by the rust equations, the water/oxygen/salt test-tube experiment, galvanic corrosion with the area rule, coatings (paint, tin, zinc), cathodic protection of a buried pipe, passivation of Al/Cr/Ti and stainless steel, and lemon and seawater cells as corrosion with the wire on the outside. Capstone: a ship-hull simulator (dry dock/river/sea, steel or bronze propeller, paint state, zinc or magnesium anodes or impressed current with a dose slider) that animates which metal dissolves and plots steel loss over 20 years with a labelled toy model. Hooks for later lessons: O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻ as the air cathode (zinc–air, fuel cells), 'the anode metal is consumed' (every primary cell), passivating films (aluminium, the SEI layer), and hydrogen evolution from surplus electrons (electrolysis, overcharge).
